finishes.headline: Three kinds of stain. Here's the honest difference.

transparent.name: Transparent / toner
transparent.look: Almost all grain. A light tint.
transparent.bestFor: New or nice wood you want to show off. Needs the most frequent recoats.

semi-transparent.name: Semi-transparent
semi-transparent.bestFor: Most deck floors. Fades instead of peeling, so recoats are easy.

solid.name: Solid color
solid.look: Even color, like paint. Texture only.
solid.bestFor: Railings, fences and patched or mismatched wood. Can peel on floors.

faq.headline: What homeowners ask us most
faq.intro: Straight answers, with links to the experts where it matters. More in our [Learn](/learn/) section.

items.q: How much does deck staining cost in {city}?
items.a: Nationally, Angi puts a typical job at $550–$1,250, about $850 on average, or roughly $2 to $4 per square foot ([Angi, 2026](source:angi)). Your price depends on size, railings, stairs and how much prep the wood needs. Our price calculator gives you a range in about a minute.

items.q: How often does a deck need to be restained?
items.a: Most sources say every two to three years for a deck floor ([Angi](source:angi)). The U.S. Forest Products Lab gives semi-transparent stain about 2–3 years on new smooth decking and 3–6 years on weathered wood ([USDA FPL](source:usdaSouth)). Shade, sun and use change that.

items.q: When is the best time of year to stain a deck in {city}?
items.a: {bestMonths}. {driestMonth} is the driest month on average here, and {fewestRainDays} have the fewest rainy days ([NOAA normals](source:climate)). Stain needs dry wood and a few dry days.

The experts disagree. The U.S. Forest Products Lab says film finishes like solid stain tend to peel on decks ([USDA FPL](source:usdaFinishes)). Consumer Reports says solid scores best in their testing ([via KOMO](source:consumerReports)). We usually suggest semi-transparent on floors and solid on railings, if you want solid.
Not the way most people mean it. High pressure can strip wood fibers off the surface ([USDA FPL](source:usdaFinishes)). We use cleaners and low pressure, then a brightener.

items.q: Can you give me a price from photos?
items.a: Yes. That's how most of our estimates start. Upload up to five photos, including one wide shot of the whole deck, and we'll send a price range. We confirm it in person or by video before we start.

In {licenseCounty}, {stateName} requires a Home Improvement license for residential jobs from $3,000 to $24,999 ([TN.gov](source:tnHomeImprovement)). Our license and insurance are listed at the bottom of every page.

items.q: Do I need to be home?
items.a: No. We just need access to the deck, a water spigot, and pets kept inside. We'll text you when we start, when we finish each day, and before we leave.

infoBoxes.title: Why does it look different from the can?
infoBoxes.text: Stain soaks into wood, so the wood's own color shows through, especially on semi-transparent. Old gray wood, new yellow pine and red cedar all take the same stain differently. This tool keeps your wood's grain and light and dark spots, so it's closer to real than a color chip.

infoBoxes.title: Is my photo private?
infoBoxes.text: Yes. The image stays on your device while you work. It's only sent to us if you fill in the form to get the full-size image. See our [privacy page](/privacy/).

infoBoxes.title: Tips for a good photo
infoBoxes.text: Shoot in daylight but not in harsh noon sun. Stand back far enough to get the whole deck. Sweep the leaves off first if you can. Wet boards look darker, so wait until it's dry.

services.name: Deck Staining
services.photoAlt: Freshly stained hardwood deck boards seen from above
services.seoDescription: Professional deck staining in {city}: low-pressure wash, brightener, two coats brushed in by hand. Sample pricing from {semiFrom}/sq ft. Free photo estimates.
services.lede: We wash, we brighten, we stain. Most decks take two days.
services.intro: Most decks we see around {city} aren't ruined. They're gray, a little rough, maybe green on the shady side. Under that is good wood that just needs the right prep and a stain that soaks in.

steps.title: Protect
steps.text: Cover plants, siding and anything we don't want stain on. Move furniture and grills (and put them back).

steps.title: Wash
steps.text: Low-pressure wash with a cleaner that lifts gray and mildew. No blasting soft wood.

steps.title: Brighten
steps.text: Brightener evens out the color and opens the grain so stain soaks in evenly.

steps.title: Dry
steps.text: We let it dry. Usually overnight at least, longer in shade. This is the step most people rush.

steps.title: Stain
steps.text: Penetrating stain, applied and back-brushed board by board. Rails and spindles by hand.

steps.title: Walk-through
steps.text: We walk it with you, touch up anything you point out, and leave care instructions.

faq.q: How long until we can use the deck?
faq.a: Light foot traffic usually the next day. Furniture back in 24–48 hours depending on the product and weather. We'll tell you for your exact stain.

faq.q: Do you sand?
faq.a: Only where it helps: raised grain, rough patches, splinters. Sanding a whole deck smooth can actually keep stain from soaking in, so we don't do it by default.

faq.q: What if it rains?
faq.a: We watch the forecast closely and reschedule if needed. If rain surprises us before the stain sets, we come back and fix it. That's on us.

services.name: Deck Cleaning & Restoration
services.photoAlt: Gray, weathered deck boards that need cleaning
services.seoTitle: Deck Cleaning & Restoration in {city} — Wash, Strip, Brighten, Sand | {short}
services.seoDescription: Deck restoration in {city}: remove peeling stain, clean mildew, brighten gray wood and sand rough boards — then seal it right. Photo estimates.
services.lede: Gray, green or peeling? That deck can come back.
services.intro: Restoration is everything that happens before the stain goes on. It's the difference between a finish that lasts and one that peels by next summer.

steps.title: Wash
steps.text: For faded and mildewed decks: a cleaner that kills the green and lifts the gray, rinsed at low pressure.

steps.title: Strip
steps.text: For peeling or failing finish: a stripper that softens the old coat so it rinses off without gouging the wood.

steps.title: Brighten
steps.text: Neutralizes the stripper or cleaner and brings the wood back to an even, fresh color.

steps.title: Sand
steps.text: Spot-sanding for raised grain, splinters and rough board ends.

steps.title: Repair
steps.text: Reset popped nails, swap cracked boards, tighten loose rails. Priced per item, no surprises.

steps.title: Seal
steps.text: Finish with the right stain for your wood and how you use the deck.

faq.q: Why not just pressure-wash it?
faq.a: High pressure tears up soft wood. The U.S. Forest Products Lab warns that power washing can remove wood from the surface. We use cleaners and low pressure instead.

faq.q: How do I know if mine needs stripping?
faq.a: If the old coat is peeling, flaking or blotchy, it needs to come off. If it's just faded and gray, a wash and brightener is usually enough. Photos tell us a lot.

faq.q: Can you fix a few bad boards?
faq.a: Yes. We replace individual boards and note them on the estimate. For structural problems (posts, joists, ledger), we'll tell you and refer you to a deck builder.

services.name: Fence Staining
services.photoAlt: Close-up of cedar fence boards with ivy
services.seoTitle: Fence Staining in {city} — Privacy, Picket & Board Fences | {short}
services.seoDescription: Wood fence staining in {city}. We spray and back-brush both sides so stain soaks in. Bundle with your deck to save on setup.
services.lede: Fences are vertical, so a good stain lasts longer on them than on a deck floor.
services.intro: A wood fence is a lot of square footage, and most of it has never been sealed. Done right once, a fence stays easy to keep up.

steps.title: Clean
steps.text: Wash off gray, mildew and dirt so the stain soaks into wood, not grime.

steps.title: Protect
steps.text: Cover plants, AC units, cars and the neighbor's side if we're only doing yours.

steps.title: Spray & back-brush
steps.text: We spray to cover fast, then brush it in. Spray-only jobs look fine for a season and then fade unevenly.

steps.title: Both sides
steps.text: Priced per side. Ask your neighbor. Many split the cost of the other side.

faq.q: How is fence staining priced?
faq.a: By the linear foot and height, per side. Send a photo and the rough length and we'll give you a range.

faq.q: Can my fence match my deck?
faq.a: Yes, but fences and decks often look different with the same stain because the wood and sun are different. We'll test it first.

services.name: Log Home & Cabin Staining
services.photoAlt: Log cabin with a covered porch and stacked firewood
services.seoTitle: Log Home & Cabin Staining in {city} and the Mountains | {short}
services.seoDescription: Log home and cabin staining around {city}: cleaning, old finish removal, and stain made for logs. {cabinAreas}.
services.lede: Logs move, check and drink stain. They need their own plan.
services.intro: Log walls take more weather than a deck rail and soak up more stain than you'd guess. We clean them, deal with the old finish, and stain them so water runs off instead of in.

steps.title: Inspect
steps.text: Look for soft spots, open checks on the top side of logs, and chinking gaps. We'll show you what we find.

steps.title: Clean
steps.text: Gentle wash for dirt, pollen and mildew. Strip failing finish where needed.

steps.title: Stain
steps.text: A log-home stain applied heavy enough to protect and brushed into checks and end grain.

steps.title: Trim & porches
steps.text: Doors, window trim, porch posts and decks matched to the walls.

faq.q: How often do log homes need restaining?
faq.a: It depends on sun, overhangs and the product. South and west walls wear fastest. We'll look at each side and tell you which ones need it now.

faq.q: Do you do chinking?
faq.a: We handle small chinking repairs as part of a stain job. For a full re-chink we'll refer you to a specialist.

services.name: Pergolas, Porches & Gazebos
services.photoAlt: Stained timber pavilion posts and floor with fall trees behind
services.seoDescription: Staining for pergolas, porches, gazebos, arbors and swing sets in {city}. Hand-brushed posts and beams, matched to your deck.
services.lede: All the posts, beams and slats that a sprayer misses.
services.intro: Pergolas and gazebos have a lot of edges and end grain, and that's where water gets in. We take the time to brush every face, including the tops of beams you can't see from the ground.

steps.title: Overhead work
steps.text: Ladders and staging for beams and rafters. We protect the floor and furniture underneath.

steps.title: End grain first
steps.text: Cut ends soak up water the fastest, so we seal them first and heaviest.

steps.title: Porch floors
steps.text: Covered porch floors get a finish suited to foot traffic and the occasional muddy boot.

steps.title: Match the deck
steps.text: If we're doing the deck too, we'll match or coordinate colors.

faq.q: Can you stain a cedar swing set or playset?
faq.a: Yes. We use a product suited to it and let it cure properly before the kids are back on it.

faq.q: My porch floor is painted. Can you stain it?
faq.a: Sometimes. Tongue-and-groove porch floors are often meant to be painted. We'll tell you honestly which finish fits.

services.name: Maintenance Plans
services.photoAlt: Brush applying finish to bare wood
services.seoTitle: Deck Maintenance Plans in {city} — Prices Shown | {short}
services.seoDescription: Deck maintenance plans in {city} with real prices: yearly check-ups and maintenance coats every 2–3 years so you never pay to strip a deck again.
services.lede: The cheapest deck to stain is one that never needs stripping.
services.intro: A maintenance coat on a faded deck costs a fraction of a full restoration. The trick is doing it on time. Pick a plan and we keep track of it for you.

steps.title: We remember
steps.text: We track when your deck was done and reach out before it's due. You don't have to think about it.

steps.title: Same color, same product
steps.text: We keep notes on exactly what's on your deck, so every coat matches.

steps.title: Priority dates
steps.text: Plan customers get first pick of fall dates, our busiest season.

steps.title: Warranty stays active
steps.text: Staying on schedule keeps your warranty going.

faq.q: What's the difference between a maintenance coat and a full job?
faq.a: A full job may include stripping, heavy cleaning, brightening and two coats. A maintenance coat is a gentle wash and one fresh coat over finish that's still sound. It's faster and costs much less.

faq.q: Can I cancel?
faq.a: Yes. Yearly plans can be cancelled any time before the next visit is booked. Monthly plans can be cancelled with 30 days' notice.

faq.q: Are these real prices?
faq.a: On this demo site they are sample prices. Each Pro Partner sets their own in the site settings.

areas.name: Farragut
areas.headline: Deck staining in Farragut subdivisions and lake homes
areas.lede: West Knox County is mostly neighborhoods built from the '80s on, plus homes on Fort Loudoun Lake. The decks are big and the HOAs are particular.
areas.photoAlt: Close view of wood deck boards

sections.headline: Second and third finishes
sections.text: Most Farragut decks are on their second or third stain job. If the last one was solid color and it's peeling, it has to come off before we start again. If it was semi-transparent, a good wash and a fresh coat is often all it takes.

sections.headline: Working with your HOA
sections.text: Many neighborhoods here have approved color lists. Send it to us and try the colors on your own deck in the visualizer before you turn in the request.

sections.headline: Fort Loudoun Lake homes
sections.text: Waterfront decks get morning fog and full afternoon sun off the lake. We plan for that with a mildew-resistant, well-pigmented stain and an honest schedule for touch-ups.

faq.q: Can you give me something to show my HOA?
faq.a: Yes. We'll send the color name and a picture of it on your deck from our visualizer, and bring a sample board if they want one.

areas.name: Powell
areas.headline: Deck staining in Powell
areas.lede: North Knox County mixes older homes on bigger lots with newer subdivisions. A lot of the decks here have never been finished at all.
areas.photoAlt: Wide wood deck with a bench

sections.headline: Never-stained decks
sections.text: We see a lot of pressure-treated decks in Powell that went straight from the builder to the weather. Gray and rough isn't the end. Cleaning and brightening usually brings them right back, and then they take stain well.

sections.headline: Fences and outbuildings
sections.text: Bigger lots mean longer fences and the occasional shed or barn. If we're already set up for the deck, adding the fence is the cheapest time to do it.

sections.headline: Quick quotes from photos
sections.text: Send a wide shot of the deck and a couple of close-ups. Most Powell decks we can price without a visit.

faq.q: My deck is 8 years old and never stained. Too late?
faq.a: Almost never. Unless boards are soft, a proper cleaning and brightener gets it ready for stain.

areas.name: Maryville
areas.headline: Deck staining in Maryville with a view of the Smokies
areas.lede: Blount County homes face the mountains, so the decks face west and south, straight into the afternoon sun.
areas.photoAlt: Wood deck and railing overlooking a wooded mountain valley

sections.headline: Sun is the main enemy here
sections.text: A deck that faces the mountains usually faces the sun all afternoon. UV breaks finish down faster than rain. We lean toward a semi-transparent with good pigment, and away from clear sealers, which tend to quit after a season in full sun.

sections.headline: Tall decks on sloped lots
sections.text: Hillside homes mean tall decks with long stairs. We price stairs and railings on their own lines so there's no guessing.

sections.headline: Around the college and downtown
sections.text: Older homes near downtown and Maryville College often have porches with years of paint. We'll tell you whether yours wants stain or paint.

woodNotes: West- and south-facing decks in full sun
Tall decks and long stairs on slopes

faq.q: Why does my mountain-view deck fade so fast?
faq.a: Because it faces the sun all afternoon. More pigment in the stain helps. So does a maintenance coat every couple of years before it wears through.

areas.name: Seymour
areas.headline: Cabin and deck staining in Seymour and the foothills
areas.lede: On the way to the mountains: log homes, cabins and a lot of rental properties with decks that get heavy use.

sections.headline: Log homes and cabins
sections.text: Logs check, move and soak up stain. We clean them, deal with the old finish, and brush stain into the checks and end grain where water gets in.

sections.headline: Rental cabin owners
sections.text: If you rent your cabin, a tired deck shows up in guest photos. Tell us your open dates and we'll schedule the work between bookings, weather permitting.

sections.headline: Hot tubs and grills
sections.text: Cabin decks often have hot tubs and grills sitting on them. We work around them, and we'll point out any boards that are getting soft under the tub.

faq.q: Can you work between cabin rentals?
faq.a: Yes. Give us the open dates. Most cabin decks are two days; log walls take longer and we'll plan for that.

areas.name: Oak Ridge
areas.headline: Deck staining in Oak Ridge
areas.lede: Oak Ridge was built fast in the 1940s. A lot of those small original homes have decks that were added decades later, and they need careful work.
areas.photoAlt: Deck with wooden railing and chairs

sections.headline: Add-on decks on older homes
sections.text: Many of the original houses got their decks later, built by different people over the years. We check the boards and rails before we stain and point out anything loose. A new finish shouldn't hide a problem.

sections.headline: Wooded lots
sections.text: The ridges are heavily wooded, so plenty of decks sit in shade and collect leaves. Expect a longer cleaning day and a mildew-resistant stain.

sections.headline: Near Melton Hill Lake
sections.text: Homes near the lake deal with more moisture. We'll suggest a maintenance plan so you're recoating on time instead of stripping later.

faq.q: Is it worth staining an old add-on deck?
faq.a: If the frame is solid, yes. Cleaning, staining and a few new boards cost a fraction of a rebuild. If it isn't safe, we'll say so.

articles.title: The best time to stain a deck in {city}
articles.description: Why {bestMonths} are the best months to stain a deck in {city}, with NOAA rainfall numbers and what the wood needs to dry.

body.lede: Short answer: **{bestMonths}**. Spring is our second choice. Midsummer and winter are the hardest. Here's why.

body.h2: Stain needs dry wood and a few dry days

body: Stain has to soak into the wood. If the boards are wet, it can't. The U.S. Forest Products Laboratory, the government's wood research lab, says to let a deck dry for at least two warm, windy days after cleaning before you finish it{cite:usdaFinishes}. Home Depot's guide for pressure-treated wood says to let it dry 24 hours after cleaning{cite:homeDepot}. On a shady deck in a humid valley, we lean toward the longer number.
So the real question is: *when does {city} give you a run of dry days?*
{city} averages about **{annualRain} inches of rain a year**. The driest months on average are {driestMonths}, and {fewestRainDays} have the fewest rainy days{cite:climate}.

That lines up with what we see on the job. Fall gives us dry spells, cooler afternoons and less direct heat on the boards. Stain that goes on in mild weather soaks in evenly instead of flashing dry on the surface.

July is one of the wettest months here on average, and pop-up afternoon storms are common. Hot boards also dry the stain too fast, which leaves lap marks. We still work in summer, but we start early, work in the shade side first, and watch the radar.

Most stains need air and wood temperatures above about 50°F while they dry. Check the label of the product you're using. Winter days are short and the boards stay damp in the morning. We use winter for estimates and booking.
Average humidity here is {humidity}{cite:humidity}. Humidity slows drying, which is one more reason we don't rush the wait between washing and staining.

checklist: Book early for {bestMonths}. Those slots fill first.
Spring works well too once the pollen settles.
If your deck is peeling or gray now, get it on the calendar. Waiting another season usually means more prep and a bigger bill.

articles.title: Oil vs. water-based deck stain: the honest answer
articles.description: Oil-based and water-based deck stains compared in plain English: how long they last, how they wear, and which is easier to redo.

body.lede: You'll hear strong opinions on this. The truth is the experts don't fully agree, and the "right" answer depends on how you want to take care of the deck later.

body: Fine Homebuilding says most water-based stains actually *last longer* than oil-based ones, about two to three years. The catch is that when they do wear out, you often have to remove the old coat completely before recoating. Oil-based stains need refinishing more often, but the touch-up is easier{cite:fineHomebuilding}.
Bob Vila's cost guide puts it the other way, with oil-based lasting about 3 to 5 years and water-based about 2 to 3{cite:bobvila}.
Both are reputable. The difference comes from the products tested, the climate, and how "lasting" gets measured. That's why we don't sell one answer to everybody.

body.h2: How they wear, in plain words

compare.title: Oil-based
items: Soaks deep into the wood and brings out the grain
Wears away slowly. It fades more than it peels.
Easy to recoat: clean it and add a coat where it's thin{cite:fineHomebuilding}
Stronger smell, slower to dry, harder cleanup

compare.title: Water-based
items: Holds its color well and dries fast
Low odor and easy cleanup
Can last longer between coats{cite:fineHomebuilding}
When it's done, it may need to be stripped first

body: For most decks around {city}, we like a **penetrating, semi-transparent** stain, oil or a modern water-based "hybrid," and a maintenance coat every couple of years. The Forest Products Lab recommends penetrating finishes over film-forming ones for decks{cite:usdaFinishes}. If you want to keep the cost of upkeep low, choose the product that's easiest to recoat. That way your second coat in three years is a quick wash-and-stain, not a strip job.

body.h2: Already have a finish on there?

body: Stay with the same type if it's in good shape. Putting water-based over oil, or oil over a film that's still on the wood, is a common reason a new coat fails. When we're not sure what's on a deck, we test a spot first.

articles.title: Semi-transparent vs. solid stain on a deck
articles.description: The government wood lab says avoid solid stain on decks. Consumer Reports says solid scores best. Here is how to decide.

body.lede: This is the one question where two trusted sources give opposite advice. We'll show you both and tell you how we decide on the job.

body: The U.S. Forest Products Laboratory has studied wood finishes for decades. Their advice for decks is clear: use **penetrating** finishes, not film-forming ones. They write that paints and solid-color stains "are prone to trap moisture and fail by peeling"{cite:usdaFinishes}. Another of their guides says paint and solid-color stains "are not appropriate for fully exposed decks"{cite:usdaSouth}, and a third says opaque stains shouldn't be used on decks and fences{cite:usdaFinishing}.
Their own table gives semi-transparent stain on decking about 2–3 years on new smooth wood and 3–6 years on weathered, rougher wood{cite:usdaSouth}.

Consumer Reports tests deck stains on panels outdoors. Their tester told KOMO News that "solid color staining always fares best in our testing," and that a solid color can last seven to 10 years, while clearer stains may need redoing every one to three years{cite:consumerReports}.

They're measuring different things. Consumer Reports rates how the finish *looks and protects* over time on test panels. The Forest Products Lab focuses on how the finish *fails* on a real deck, where water gets in at the board ends, cracks and nail holes. When a solid stain does fail on a floor, it peels, and peeling means stripping. When a semi-transparent wears, it fades, and fading means a quick recoat.

compare.title: We lean semi-transparent when…
items: It's a walking surface: deck floors, stairs
The deck is shady or damp (think {shadyArea})
You want to see the wood grain
You want cheap, easy maintenance coats

compare.title: Solid can make sense when…
items: It's vertical: railings, skirting, fences, siding
The wood is mismatched or patched and you want one even color
You understand a failed solid coat means stripping later
There's good airflow and drainage

body: A popular middle path: **semi-transparent on the floor, solid on the railings.** You get a grain look underfoot and a crisp, long-lasting color on the parts you look at most.
Our written warranty reflects this. Solid stain on deck floors gets a shorter term, and we tell you why up front.

articles.title: New pressure-treated deck? When to stain it
articles.description: How long to wait before staining a new pressure-treated deck, the 10-minute sprinkle test, and why waiting too long costs you.

body.lede: Brand-new deck? Don't stain it the day the builder leaves, and don't wait three years either.

body: Pressure-treated lumber comes from the yard wet. Home Depot's guide says it can take several weeks to dry{cite:homeDepot}. Stain put on wet wood can't soak in. It sits on top and flakes off.
The Forest Products Lab's deck guide says wood that was treated with a water repellent at the factory, or recently treated, should weather for about 2 to 3 months before finishing{cite:usdaFinishes}.

steps: Sprinkle some water on a few boards in the sun and a few in the shade.
If it soaks in, the wood is ready. Plan to stain soon. If it beads up or pools, give it more time{cite:homeDepot}.

body: One exception: lumber stamped **KDAT** (kiln dried after treatment) has already been dried and can be stained right away{cite:homeDepot}.

body.h2: Why you don't wait too long

body: Bare wood in the sun turns gray within a season or two. That gray layer is damaged surface fiber. Stain won't stick well to it until it's cleaned and brightened, which adds a step and cost. The Forest Products Lab notes that most decks are retired early because of cracks and checks that timely finishing could have prevented{cite:usdaFinishes}.

body.h2: Our advice for a new deck

checklist: Do the sprinkle test every few weeks after the deck is built.
When it passes, book the first coat. For most decks that's within the first year.
Ask about a maintenance plan. A new deck is the cheapest one to keep looking new.

articles.title: Why deck stain peels (and how to stop it)
articles.description: The real reasons deck stain peels: film finishes, wet wood, and coating over old finish. Plus what fixes it for good.

body.lede: Peeling is the number one complaint we hear. It's almost never bad luck. There are a few causes, and they're all fixable.

body.h2: 1. A film finish on a walking surface

body: Paints and solid stains form a film on top of the wood. The Forest Products Lab says film-forming finishes on decks are prone to trap moisture and fail by peeling{cite:usdaFinishes}. Semi-transparent stains, by comparison, won't blister or peel even if water gets into the wood{cite:usdaFinishes}. They fade instead.

Stain on damp wood can't grip. That happens when someone stains the day after a rain, the morning after washing, or on brand-new lumber that hasn't dried. The lab recommends at least two warm, windy days of drying after cleaning{cite:usdaFinishes}.

body.h2: 3. New coat on top of a failing coat

body: If the old finish is lifting, a new coat on top is only as strong as what's underneath. It peels right along with it. This is the most common mistake we fix.
More isn't better. Penetrating stain should soak in. The extra that sits in puddles on top dries into a soft film that scuffs and flakes. We back-brush and wipe off any excess before it dries.

A high-pressure wash can tear up soft wood. The lab warns that aggressive scrubbing or power washing can remove wood from the surface{cite:usdaFinishes}. That fuzzy surface takes stain unevenly. We wash with low pressure and the right cleaner, and let the chemistry do the work.

steps: Strip what's failing, all of it, down to sound wood.
Brighten the wood so it's open and even.
Apply a penetrating stain and back-brush it in.
Recoat on schedule, before it wears through.

body: Stripping is the most work we do, so a peeling deck costs more than one that's just faded. Our [price calculator](/pricing/) shows the difference when you choose "Peeling."

articles.title: How often to restain a deck in {stateName} humidity
articles.description: How many years a deck stain really lasts in {stateName}: what Angi, Bob Vila and the U.S. Forest Products Lab say, and what changes it.

body.lede: Most decks around here want attention every **two to three years**. Railings and fences can usually go longer. Here's what the sources say, and what moves the number up or down.

head: Source
What they say
rows: Restain every two to three years
Semi-transparent on decking: 2–3 years on new smooth wood, 3–6 years on weathered rough wood
Clear water-repellent sealers: about 1 year on exposed deck surfaces

body: Those are averages. The lab's own table says its numbers are for an average location in the continental United States{cite:usdaSouth}. {city} isn't average.

We get about {annualRain} inches of rain a year here{cite:climate}, and average humidity is {humidity}{cite:humidity}. Wet wood that dries slowly grows mildew, and mildew breaks down a finish from the top. Add strong summer sun on open decks and you get wear from both sides.

body.h2: What makes yours last longer or shorter

compare.title: Shorter
items: Full afternoon sun on the deck floor
Heavy shade and leaf piles
Clear or very light finishes (less pigment, less UV protection)
Dogs, grills, planters, kids

compare.title: Longer
items: Vertical surfaces: railings, fences, siding
Good airflow under and around the deck
Semi-transparent with good pigment
A yearly wash and a quick check

body.h2: The cheapest way to keep a deck nice

body: Recoat *before* it wears through. A maintenance coat on a faded deck costs a fraction of stripping a failed one. That's the whole idea behind our [maintenance plans](/services/maintenance-plans/), and why our dashboard reminds us to call you before your deck needs it.
And check the structure while you're at it. The North American Deck and Railing Association recommends homeowners check their deck every year{cite:nadra}.
